mappings.note: Asks for the term used for ionic compounds INSTEAD of molecular mass. That is LO-39's final differentiation pair, 'formula unit mass and molecular mass', in one line. Not LO-41: nothing is computed, only the right term chosen.
Na2O formula unit mass, 62 u. Straight LO-41 arithmetic; the item never asks why the term is 'formula unit', which is what would add LO-39.

Explain the law using the barium chloride reaction as an illustration. Explanation with a worked example is LO-40 - distinct from fe7c301a, which asks the student to DESCRIBE THE ACTIVITY and lands on LO-39's verification clause, and from c1b1d1ce, which only states the law (LO-48).

Three Dalton postulates and how each underwrites a law of chemical combination. LO-40 covers Dalton's theory, conservation of mass and constant proportions in one row, so this item is entirely inside it.

What polyatomic ions are and how their valency is used in a formula. The graded end is formula construction, LO-42. LO-39 was considered for the 'what is a polyatomic ion' half but the item never sets it against a monatomic ion.

Defines a chemical bond and asks for the energy change on bonding. LO-40 carries the bond-formation half. Flagged as a genuinely poor fit: bond energy appears nowhere in this curriculum - not in any learning outcome and not in competency C1.1's text - so the second half of this item is unmapped.
Draw O2's electron dots and explain why the bond must be double. Covalent formation, LO-40; the double bond has no outcome of its own, so it shares the code with the single-bond items.
The rules for an ionic formula containing a polyatomic ion, worked on aluminium sulfate. LO-42; this is the extended version of the MCQ 7ffa4cd3 and shares its outcome.

Why 'formula unit mass' is preferred over 'molecular mass' for ionic solids. The demand is exactly LO-39's molecular-mass-versus-formula-unit-mass pair, resolved by structure. Not LO-41: the item explains the terminology instead of computing anything.
Ionic melting and boiling points explained against covalent ones, by reference to lattice structure. Explicit two-class comparison, the cleanest kind of LO-39 item in the chapter.

Define molecular mass and compute it step by step for water. Definition plus calculation both sit inside LO-41, which names molecular mass; no comparison with formula unit mass is asked, so LO-39 is not added.
Draw Cl2's electron sharing and say what bond results and why. Covalent formation, LO-40, in the same family as the O2 and H2 drawings.

Two demands: state the law of constant proportions (LO-48, familiarity) and then show how water's fixed composition illustrates it (LO-40, explanation). This item is the reason the two codes are kept distinct across the chapter - here it asks for both.

Draw the electron transfer that makes NaCl and name the structure the ions then adopt. Formation of an ionic compound through to its lattice, LO-40. The structural half alone would be LO-39 only if it were being contrasted with molecular compounds, which it is not.

Defining cations against anions is LO-39's cation/anion pair; explaining the electrostatic force that then binds them is LO-40's ionic formation clause. The item needs both and neither alone answers it.

Why the baking soda is kept in the balloon before the start mass is taken, and what the balance will read afterwards. Pure experimental design and prediction - LO-39's fused 'plan and demonstrate activities to observe and verify' clause, and the strongest short-answer instance of it.
Prefix naming rules plus why dihydrogen monoxide is called water. Nomenclature conventions, LO-42. The traditional-name half is the same point as MCQ 1e17a88b about ammonia.
What formula unit mass represents, then compute it for KCl. Both halves inside LO-41, which names formula unit mass. Contrast 84e5727c, which asks why the TERM differs and therefore goes to LO-39.
Define a covalent bond and explain H2's formation. Formation outcome, LO-40 - the same pairing the frame itself makes by putting the definition and the formation of covalent compounds in one row.

Predict and explain what the conductivity rig does with an NaCl solution. Property-based identification of an ionic compound, LO-39. Not LO-39's activity clause: the apparatus here tests conductivity, not conservation of mass.

What determines an atom's stability and why noble gases stay monoatomic. Mapped to LO-40's formation clause read in the negative. Flagged: the octet rule and valence-shell stability are named only inside competency C1.1's descriptive text and in no learning outcome, so this whole sub-family sits on LO-40 by extension rather than by wording.

First half tells an ion from its neutral parent atom (LO-39's cation/anion clause); second half explains how neutral sodium becomes Na+ (LO-40's formation clause). Its neighbour 1dc77aeb asks only the second half and takes LO-40 alone.

Defends constant proportions against the CO/CO2 counterexample - the law binds each compound separately. Explanation under challenge, LO-40. C1.2 is not added because the confusion here is between two compounds, not between a compound and a mixture, which is what separates this from 3d544a1c and 81ec9229.
Draw sodium and its cation and say why the atom gives the electron up. The 'why' is the formation driver, LO-40; the shell diagram is a means, not the graded end, so LO-41 is not cited.

Rebut the claim that covalent compounds have high melting points by separating intramolecular bonds from intermolecular forces. A property-based ionic/covalent discrimination, LO-39, and the most demanding one in that family.
